blockers: No executable Quidra concurrency workload/program was available under the readable template paths to empirically exercise task.all/atomic.Counter; assessment is documentation-only.
findings: The standard-namespace list explicitly reserves `task` and `atomic` as concurrency-related namespaces alongside `ref`, `gpu`, etc.

'Implementation scope' explicitly states the native core supports 'bounded structured concurrency through task.all for capture-free effect-only operations, ordered int[] / float[] scalar results, and explicit atomic.Counter shared state.'

This documents a narrow, structured-concurrency-only model: task.all is a bounded fork-join primitive over capture-free (no closures capturing mutable outer state) effect-only tasks, producing ordered int[]/float[] aggregated results, plus one atomic counter type for shared mutable state.
'Cancellation' is explicitly listed as a remaining development area, implying task.all currently lacks cancellation support.

No general-purpose thread spawning, channels/message-passing, async/await syntax, futures/promises, actor model, or general shared-mutable-state primitives (locks, mutexes, condition variables, general atomics beyond Counter) are documented anywhere in the spec.

The `&` reference/address model is carefully specified for sequential-code aliasing safety, but the spec does not describe how its flow-sensitive guarantees interact with concurrent tasks, suggesting the safety model for concurrency is currently narrow and task.all-scoped rather than a general data-race-freedom guarantee across arbitrary code (unlike e.g. Rust Send/Sync).

GPU work is documented as host-asynchronous by default with explicit synchronization points (gpu.sync, .cpu(), .item(), time.now(sync=true)/time.since(sync=true)) -- a real, well-designed asynchronous execution model, but this is device-offload asynchrony rather than general CPU-side concurrency/parallelism for arbitrary user code.
metric.concurrency.method: Documentation review of the same spec files for concurrency primitives: task.*, atomic.*, thread/goroutine/actor/async keywords.
metric.concurrency.normalization_rationale: Scored 32/100. Reflects a genuinely present, safety-oriented but intentionally narrow concurrency model: bounded structured fork-join via task.all restricted to capture-free effect-only tasks, one atomic counter type, no cancellation, no channels/actors/async-await, no general thread/lock primitives. This is materially less expressive than mainstream languages with mature concurrency models (e.g. goroutines+channels, async/await with Send/Sync, structured concurrency with cancellation, virtual threads), while still nonzero because task.all + atomic.Counter + explicit GPU async/sync primitives constitute a real, coherent, if minimal, concurrency design.

blockers: No FFI example program was available under the readable template paths; assessment is documentation-only against the frozen language spec.
findings: No 'extern', 'ffi', 'foreign', 'cdecl', 'dlopen', or C-ABI declaration syntax appears anywhere in the documented surface language.

The 'Implementation scope' section explicitly enumerates what the native core currently supports (fixed-width numerics, casts, bin, arrays, tensors, image I/O, console I/O, namespaces, generics, classes, function values, bounded structured concurrency via task.all, atomic.Counter) and does not list any FFI/foreign-function/native-library-binding capability.

That same section names remaining development areas explicitly ('Cancellation, broader managed result transfer, self-hosting, broader signal-processing APIs, and broader package distribution') without naming general native interoperability as present or planned.

'bin' is a packed raw-bit-sequence value type with explicit conversions to/from integers, bools, and flat arrays -- a plausible building block for a future binary/ABI marshaling layer -- but no calling convention, symbol linkage, header/binding generation, or foreign memory-ownership model is specified.

GPU/tensor sections describe explicit internal integration with backend-native libraries (CUDA Driver API, HIP runtime, Metal), but this is compiler/runtime-internal device integration, not a general user-facing mechanism for calling arbitrary C/C++ libraries from Quidra source.
No FFI declaration form, header import, or native shared-library linkage story appears in any of the readable spec documents.
metric.ffi_interoperability_design.method: Documentation review of repo/docs/spec/language.md and architecture.md (frozen snapshot spec, version 0.2). Searched for FFI/extern/C-ABI/native-library-binding surface.
metric.ffi_interoperability_design.normalization_rationale: Scored 15/100. Reflects a language with a coherent explicit-boundary-crossing philosophy (address/reference model, explicit bin<->numeric conversions, explicit CPU/GPU transfer boundaries) that could underlie a future FFI design, but no documented general-purpose FFI/native-interop mechanism exists in the frozen spec to evaluate. This is a genuine language-design gap (FFI/interop design quality per the language_quality boundary rules), not an ecosystem/tooling-maturity gap, since there is no FFI syntax/semantics at all to assess, only plausible primitives it could be built from.
